    Scroll, and the stage changes with each act. Underlined words and names open a short note. Point at or tap a puppet to see where it comes from, and click a painting or statue to see it up close. Red stamps are myth-checks.

    Overture: the cards on the table

    Sit down. Cut the deck. The fortune-teller turns over three cards: the Sun, the Moon, the Star. She wears a scarf fringed with coins, gold hoops and a shawl full of stars, and she looks as if she came from somewhere far away and very old.

    That’s roughly the picture many people have of Sicily too: an island of omens and charms, of saints with goddesses under their robes, where the old gods never quite left. So let’s start with the cards, because they’re the easiest trick to see through.

    Tarot began as a card game, in the courts of 15th-century northern Italy, probably in Milan or Ferrara. The oldest surviving packs, the painted Visconti-Sforza cards, were made for the dukes of Milan between about 1440 and 1480. People played tarocchi to win tricks, not to see the future.

    The fortune-telling came three centuries later, in Paris. In 1781 the scholar Antoine Court de Gébelin announced that the cards were the lost Book of Thoth, the wisdom of ancient Egyptian priests, and that “Gypsies” had carried it into Europe. Around the same years a Paris card-reader who signed himself Etteilla (his surname, Alliette, backwards) made the first pack meant only for fortune-telling.

    Others piled on. In 1889 the Paris occultist Papus called his book The Tarot of the Bohemians. In London the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, a society of English occultists founded in 1888, redesigned the pack, and the deck most card-readers use today came out of that circle in the early 1900s.

    No one ever found evidence tying tarot to Egypt, or to the Romani people that “Gypsies” meant. The exotic origin was added to make an Italian card game look ancient and mysterious, and the costume came with it.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: tarot is ancient Egyptian or “Gypsy” wisdomWhat the record shows: an Italian card game of the 1400s; the exotic origin was invented in Paris in 1781

    And Sicily? It got tarot in the mid-1600s, probably from Rome, and went on playing it as a game. According to the card-games site Pagat, a few people in Mineo, Palagonia and Grammichele, and at Tortorici in the province of Messina, still play Sicilian tarocchi, with the island’s own small pack of 63 cards.

    The cards are a small case of something that happens to Sicily a lot: outsiders pin an ancient, exotic story on something ordinary Sicilians do. Since the 1820s writers have read the island as a place where the old gods hid inside the saints. An English writer, J. J. Blunt, set Catania’s Saint Agatha beside the goddess Ceres in 1823. Palermo’s own great folklorist, Giuseppe Pitrè, wrote in 1881 of Sicilian traditions as “remains of ancient mythologies”. British anthropologists of the same years called customs like these “survivals”, fossils of an older religion.

    There’s a reason the story sticks. Sicily is very old, and nearly everyone ruled it at some point: Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Normans, Germans, French, Spaniards. Its feasts are loud, its saints are everywhere, and its dead are close. But the goddess under every saint is mostly a 19th-century idea, and it hides the better story.

    Here’s that story. On an island one outside power after another ruled, Sicilians took the Church’s saints, relics and feasts and made them their own answers to plague, lava, hunger and death.

    Why a show in acts? Because the famous claims come in bundles, and it’s easier to check one bundle at a time. Acts 1 to 3 visit three cities and the women saints who guard them: Catania, Palermo and Messina. Act 4 sets Saint Joseph’s table. Acts 5 and 6 happen at night, with the dead who help the living and the healers the Inquisition put on trial. Act 7 opens a cabinet of relics, and Act 8 follows the saints across the ocean. The stage above changes with each act, and the red stamps mark the claims that don’t hold up.

    Where the goddess story came from

    The scholars’ word for beliefs from different sources blending into one practice is . It’s an old Greek word: Plutarch used the verb for Cretans who stopped feuding and joined forces against an outside enemy.

    In the late 1800s anthropologists such as Edward Tylor, and after him James Frazer in Britain, treated folk customs as “survivals”: leftovers of an older religion, still twitching. That idea shaped how a generation read Sicily. Most scholars now reject it as a general rule, though a few still argue for long continuity in particular beliefs.

    Three people shaped how Sicily’s folk religion is understood, and you’ll meet them again on the way:

    • , a Palermo doctor, spent decades collecting his island’s customs, and also helped start the survival story.
    • , writing in a fascist prison, argued that ordinary people’s folklore was a worldview of its own, “to be taken seriously”.
    • studied magic in mainland southern Italy in the 1950s and refused to call it a pre-Christian leftover; he tied it to Catholic practice instead.

    Why Sicily gets the spooky treatment. Part of the answer is plain prejudice. Once Sicily became part of the new Italy, many in the North saw the South as a problem to explain, and explained it the way Europe talked about the East: exotic, backward, a little mysterious. Historians call that habit Orientalism, and the scholars in Jane Schneider’s 1998 book Italy’s “Southern Question” call Italy’s version “Orientalism in one country”. One of its chapters is titled “The Magic of the South”.

    The tone was set early. In 1860 the politician Carlo Farini said of the South, “This is Africa: compared to these peasants the Bedouins are the pinnacle of civilization,” as the journalist Frank Viviano recounts. Then came race science. In 1876 the criminologist Cesare Lombroso claimed to find “African and Oriental elements” in the people of Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia, and later social scientists, Sergi and Niceforo among them, ranked Italians on a ladder of races with northerners at the top and Africa as the bottom rung. Sicily’s Arab centuries were held against it, as if a medieval past could explain a modern crime rate.

    The prejudice crossed the ocean with the emigrants. In the United States Sicilians were often treated as something less than fully white; an 1899 writer in Harper’s Weekly said they could “hardly be classed as ‘white men.’” In New Orleans, whose Italian community was mostly Sicilian, a mob killed eleven Italian prisoners in 1891, the worst mass lynching in American history, and a New York Times editorial called Sicilians “the descendants of bandits and assassins”.

    None of this made Sicilians more magical than anyone else. It made them easy to cast as the mysterious ones, and a story about goddesses hiding under the saints fit the part. It’s the fortune-teller’s costume again, this time on a whole island.

    Sicily 101: saints, relics and rulers

    If you didn’t grow up Catholic, a few words first, because the whole show runs on them.

    A saint, in Catholic belief, is a holy person who has died and is now with God. Catholics don’t worship saints as gods. They ask them to pray for them, the way you might ask a well-connected friend to put in a word. That asking is called ; the Church’s Catechism says the saints “do not cease to intercede with the Father for us”.

    The Church decides who counts. Its law allows public veneration only of those it has listed among the saints or the blessed. Hold on to that for Act 5.

    A martyr is a saint who was killed for the faith. Sicily’s oldest saints, Agatha among them, were martyrs of the Roman persecutions, at least by tradition.

    A patron saint is a town’s own protector. Around 1900 Pitrè surveyed about 150 Sicilian towns: Mary was the main patron of 45 and the Crucifix of 13, and 50 different saints shared the other 88.

    A relic is what a saint left behind: the body, a part of it, or something the saint touched. Church rules today sort relics into significant ones (the body or notable parts of it) and small ones. To a city, a relic means its saint is physically there.

    A feast, or festa, is the saint’s day, and in Sicily it means a procession: the saint’s statue or relics carried through the streets on a huge float, with the whole town out.

    Why the floats? Sicily’s four great city feasts, for Rosalia in Palermo, Agatha in Catania, the Assumption of Mary in Messina and the Good Friday Misteri in Trapani, all took their present shape in the baroque age of the 1600s and 1700s. Jesuits, trade guilds and city governments turned them into shows meant to astonish, with carts, giant candles and machines. The historian Francesco Benigno calls them “creations of the baroque”. So the floats are about 400 years old, not 2,000.

    Before the colonists came, the island belonged to , with Phoenicians trading on the coasts. Greeks founded colonies from the 8th century BC, and Rome made Sicily a province in the 3rd century BC.

    Then the island changed hands, again and again.

    Read it as a list
    • 535: Byzantium takes the island.
    • 831: Arabs take Palermo.
    • 1061–1091: the Normans conquer the island; Palermo falls in 1071–72.
    • 1130: Roger II is crowned, and the Kingdom of Sicily begins.
    • 1194–1266: the Hohenstaufen. 1266–1282: the Angevins.
    • 1282: the Sicilian Vespers, and Aragon takes over.
    • 1443: one king for Naples and Sicily again.
    • 1713: Savoy. 1720–1734: Austria. 1816: the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

    The Church didn’t need to hide inside the old gods. It moved into their buildings. In the late 6th century the Temple of Concord at Agrigento and the Athenaion at Syracuse became churches, and Palermo’s cathedral was rebuilt, from about 1170, on the site of a mosque. Reusing a building isn’t the same as keeping its religion.

    And in 1487 the Spanish Inquisition sent its first inquisitor to Sicily. Hold that thought too.

    Act 1

    Catania: Agatha goes away, and comes back

    Catania is a city on Sicily’s east coast, at the foot of Mount Etna, the volcano that towers over the island’s east. Its patron saint is Agatha, a young Christian woman of the city who, by tradition, was put to death there for her faith in the 250s, under the Roman emperor Decius. Christians were honoring her by late Roman times.

    About 1040, during his campaign of 1038–40, the Byzantine general George Maniakes took her body to Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire. No source from the time gives the year. Who received her there, the sources don’t agree: some say Emperor Michael IV, others Empress Theodora.

    On 17 August 1126 two soldiers, Gislebertus and Goselinus, brought her body home to Catania. The clergy met it “nudis pedibus et in albis vestibus”: barefoot, in white. That makes 2026 the 900th anniversary of her homecoming.

    Catania still celebrates her with the Festa di Sant’Agata, from 3 to 5 February, and again on 17 August for the return. Devotees wear a white robe, the . A lovely story says it recalls the nightshirts people ran out in when the relics came home in 1126; the historian Benigno dates the robe to the 1700s.

    Inside the silver woman. Here’s the part that startles people who didn’t grow up Catholic: Agatha isn’t buried. Most of her bones sit inside a bust of her in gilded silver, made by Giovanni di Bartolo of Siena and dated 1376 by its inscription, and so covered in donated jewellery that the silver barely shows. A piece of her pelvis is sealed inside it. In 1963 her skull was taken out so the faithful could venerate it. Her two thighbones have reliquaries of their own, inside a great relic chest. In her legend her torturers cut off her breasts, and one breast is honoured as a relic too, in the town of Galatina in Apulia, on the mainland. On her feast days the bust leaves the cathedral and is carried through the streets.

    To devotees that isn’t morbid. A saint’s body keeps the saint present in the town that holds it, close enough to be asked for help, and Catania has her. Act 7 opens the cabinet on how Europe came to collect saints this way. Her crown, by the way, is often said to be a gift from Richard the Lionheart. It was made in the late 1400s, long after his day.

    You’ll also read that this is the world’s third-largest religious festival. We found no count behind that ranking, and Catania’s own daily paper, La Sicilia, has called it a figure “never verified”, repeated for 30 years.

    Is Agatha a goddess in disguise? For Agatha the usual candidates are two goddesses. Ceres was the Roman goddess of growing crops; early on her cult merged with that of the Greek Demeter, who was widely worshipped in Sicily. Isis was one of the great goddesses of ancient Egypt, and her cult spread across the Roman Empire.

    Why them? Blunt, in 1823, set Agatha beside Ceres, and admitted he couldn’t prove it. In 1905 the historian Emanuele Ciaceri compared her feast to a procession for Isis described by the Roman writer Apuleius: crowds, white clothes, lights. A 2025 study by Cristiana Soraci answers in its title, “Né Demetra, né Iside” (neither Demeter nor Isis). At Apuleius’s procession everyone wore white; in 1126 only the clergy did. And Isis is known in Catania only from a few statuettes, a lamp and some coins.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Agatha is Ceres or Isis in disguiseWhat the record shows: first claimed in 1823 and 1905, with no evidence of a link

    The veil. Devotees believe her veil can hold back Etna’s lava. In 1669 Etna erupted for four months, from March to July. Through those months the veil and other relics were carried in prayer processions, in the villages in the lava’s path and in Catania itself, and citizens led by Diego Pappalardo tried to dig the flow aside. On 30 April the lava broke through the city walls on the west side and destroyed part of the walls and a number of buildings; it had already reached the sea at the harbor. Believers said the veil kept the whole city from being destroyed. The rest of Catania did survive the lava.

    Act 2

    Palermo: Rosalia and the plague

    In May 1624 the plague reached Palermo.

    Rosalia was a local hermit of the 12th century, as tradition tells it, with a small cult and not much else.

    Then, on 15 July 1624, bones were found in a cave on Monte Pellegrino, the mountain above the city. Tradition says the visions of a sick woman, Geronima La Gattuta of Ciminna, led the search.

    Here is the timeline, and it is the punchline.

    Read it as a list
    • 15 July 1624: bones found.
    • 27 July 1624: the Senate elects Rosalia patron of Palermo.
    • November 1624: the Church sets up a commission to check whether the bones are hers.
    • February 1625: the commission says yes.
    • 9 June 1625: the relics’ first procession.
    • 15 July 1625: the plague is declared over, one year to the day after the finding.

    The cathedral’s own account adds one more vision. On 4 February 1625 a soap-maker, Vincenzo Bonelli (some spell it Bonello), climbed Monte Pellegrino meaning to kill himself. He said Rosalia appeared to him there and asked for a procession of her relics.

    Palermo made her its patron seven months before anyone confirmed whose bones they were. Palermitans credit her with ending the plague; that is their belief, and they have kept it for four centuries.

    In 1627 Giordano Cascini published a biography of her (a saint’s life story is traditionally called a Life, in Latin a vita). About 1630 her name went into the Roman Martyrology, the Church’s official list of saints in the order of their feast days. Her relics have lain in a silver urn in the cathedral since 1631.

    Even so, she never took over the island. In Pitrè’s survey around 1900 she was the main patron of just 7 towns.

    Today the runs 10 to 15 July. On the evening of the 14th a huge decorated cart, the , carries her image through the city; on the 15th her urn of relics goes in procession. In September comes the .

    You’ll read that her cave was once a shrine to Tanit, the great goddess of Carthage, the Phoenician city across the sea. Even the scholar who suggested it wrote “probably”, and no inscription or find from the cave backs it up.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Rosalia’s cave was Tanit’s shrineWhat the record shows: no finds, no inscription

    There’s also a tale that the English geologist William Buckland declared the bones a goat’s. It comes from a memoir published in 1900, 75 years later, and no source says he ever handled them.

    Act 3

    Messina: a letter from Mary

    Messina has a feast on 3 June for a letter. The legend says Mary, the mother of Jesus, wrote to the people of Messina in the year 42, from Jerusalem, blessed their city, and tied the letter with a lock of her own hair.

    It’s a wonderful story, and a young one. The legend arose in the 16th century; the oldest text is on an engraving of 1522, and the oldest manuscript copy is from 1599. Its supporters later said the letter had been found in Greek in the 1400s and translated, but no one has shown that Greek original.

    Rome wasn’t sure either. In 1629 a scholar named Inchofer published a defense of the letter, and the Congregation of the Index, the Vatican office that censored books, objected; a corrected edition came out in 1632. The city kept its letter anyway.

    The lock of hair, kept as a relic, still rides the city’s silver in the June procession.

    Act 4

    St Joseph’s tables

    Joseph, in the Gospels, is Mary’s husband and the man who raised Jesus as his own. His feast is 19 March, and in Sicily it is a feast for the poor. Families build great tables of bread and food and feed three of the poorest people they can find, often children, dressed as Mary, Joseph and Jesus: the . The night before, bonfires: the .

    Pitrè recorded these meals for the poor by 1900 at the latest. Nobody knows exactly when they began. The folklorist Del Giudice found nothing like them in Spain or its colonies. The story you’ll hear most, of a medieval famine ended when Joseph sent rain and fava beans, turns up almost only in emigrant communities, with no source behind it.

    Sicily’s regional government keeps an official register of living traditions, the REIS (Registro delle Eredità Immateriali), begun in 2005. In its list as published in September 2013, the latest full list we could find, St Joseph had 11 of the 86 feasts and rituals, more than any other saint.

    Some writers, Pitrè among them, called the eve bonfires “certainly pagan”, and the tables a spring rite for Demeter, the Greek goddess of grain, in Christian dress. Del Giudice finds the parallels real and the descent unproven.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: the tables are a Christianized Demeter riteWhat the record shows: parallels, not descent

    Act 5 · night

    The dead who help

    Catholics pray for the dead as well as to the saints. Most people who die at peace with God, the Church teaches, aren’t ready for heaven at once; first they pass through a “final purification”, called purgatory, and the living can help them through it with prayer. Help runs the other way too. In the Catechism’s words, “our prayer for them is capable not only of helping them, but also of making their intercession for us effective.”

    In Palermo that two-way traffic found its most surprising partners: the , “the beheaded”.

    From 1541 a brotherhood in white, the Compagnia dei Bianchi, comforted everyone condemned to death in Palermo. Its members stayed with the condemned for their last three days and nights, took them in as brothers, walked with them to the scaffold, buried them and begged alms for prayers for their souls.

    Why pray to an executed criminal? Because of how he died. A condemned man who confessed and repented before the end died forgiven in the Church’s eyes, like the crucified beside Jesus. His execution paid for his crime here; purgatory would see to the rest. Pitrè, who studied the cult in the 1880s, said the people saw the repentant executed as martyrs, a Christian idea, not a pagan one.

    They were buried together by the Oreto river, at a church that was rebuilt in 1785 and again later. People said their souls walked at night along the river, dressed in white, to warn and help the living, and that if robbers attacked you on a dark road you could call on them and they would come.

    What do people ask them for? Pitrè heard prayers for help in business, for three numbers to play in the lottery, for a mother’s children to come home safe; later historians add health, and sons spared a bad death. Devotees came on Mondays and Fridays, often barefoot, to say a rosary to the souls, and those who couldn’t make the trip kept a novena, nine days of prayer, by candlelight at home. In Pitrè’s day the church walls held about a hundred painted tablets of thanks.

    Are they saints? Not to the Church: they were never listed among its saints or blessed. They were saints of the street, “popular, though not officially recognised”, as the historians Davies and Matteoni put it, and other towns had their own.

    Francesco Frusteri of Paceco, near Trapani, is one. He was a farmer who killed his own mother and was beheaded at Paceco on 5 November 1817. An inscription in the town’s church of San Francesco di Paola says he died “resigned and contrite”. Seventy years later Pitrè found him “in fame of sanctity” and heard of miracles credited to him in Trapani, Paceco and on the Isola Grande.

    The dead visit children too. On 2 November, the Day of the Dead, many Sicilian families tell children that their dead relatives come back in the night and leave presents: , sugar dolls, with fruit and nuts in a basket. You’ll read that the custom carries on Roman offerings to the dead, but nobody we found names a document for that.

    And when a saint or a soul comes through, you say thank you where everyone can see it. That’s an ex-voto, a in dialect. Painted ones show the danger, the person saved and the holy helper; wax, metal or terracotta ones show the healed body part. The Palermo scholar I. E. Buttitta calls a painted ex-voto a “standing declaration of debt” to the saint. Some writers see ancient votive terracottas in the silver limbs; the dated Sicilian painted tablets are from the 1800s and 1900s, and a resemblance isn’t a family tree.

    Act 6 · night

    Witches, healers and the evil eye

    Remember the inquisitor of 1487? The Inquisition was the Church’s court for heresy, beliefs and practices the Church judged false, and Spain ran its own version under its king. From 1487 to 1782 Sicily had a branch of it, answering to Madrid, not Rome. From 1601 it sat in the Steri palace in Palermo.

    When the court was shut down in 1782, the viceroy, Domenico Caracciolo, had its archive seized. On 27 June 1783 the papers were burned. The historian Vittorio Sciuti Russi calls it “a political bonfire” for reasons of state: people at the time said the inquisitor general, Salvatore Ventimiglia, asked for it, and the island’s nobles and senior clergy were glad to see it go, because the files showed which families had served the court. What historians use now are the yearly reports the court sent to Madrid.

    You’ll still read that thousands of witches burned in Sicily. The court’s own records say otherwise. It tried about 6,000 to 7,000 people, about 1,000 of them for magic or witchcraft. The Inquisition didn’t carry out executions itself: it handed the condemned to the king’s officials, “the secular arm”. For witchcraft it handed over two people in nearly three centuries, both men. No woman is known to have been executed as a witch.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: “thousands of witches burned in Sicily”What the record shows: two men handed over in nearly three centuries

    So who was put to death? In the early years, mostly people accused of secretly keeping the Jewish faith after converting to Christianity: before about 1540 the court handed over somewhere between 200 and 440 of them for burning, depending on the count and the years. After that the numbers fell to 25 to 52 people burned in person between 1540 and 1700, for every charge together. Many of them were Protestants, whom the court called “Lutherans”: the historian Abbate counts 36 burned alive in the 1500s, out of 253 tried. Most of the court’s everyday business was smaller. In a letter of 1652 the inquisitors said the people paraded at their public ceremonies were there “mostly” for blasphemy, bigamy and sorcery.

    The ladies from outside. The strangest things in the trial records are the , “the ladies from outside”. Sicilians described them as fairy women who went about at night in small companies. They slipped into houses “like a breath of air”, played with the children, opened the chests, ate and drank, and left a tidy house blessed. Three centuries later Pitrè called them “something of a fairy and something of a witch”, and admitted he couldn’t tell which was which. People also called them patroneddri di casa, the little masters of the house. As early as about 1450 a Sicilian handbook for confessors told priests to ask whether penitents believed in them.

    Some people, mostly poor women, said they rode with a company themselves. According to the historian Gustav Henningsen, who studied their trials, they were above all healers: if a child fell ill because the fairies had been offended, you went to someone who travelled with them, and she put it right. The companies went out on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, never Fridays or Sundays, and the fairies have names in the records: Doña Inguanta, King Cuco, Doña Zabela.

    To the inquisitors it sounded like witchcraft. In 1587 Lauria de Pavia, the elderly wife of a poor fisherman, told them she had flown, about six palms above the ground, to Benevento on the mainland, where a red-haired young man and a beautiful woman were called King and Queen. The Palermo inquisitors wrote, “If what this woman says is true … a new sect of witches has arisen.”

    Dozens stood trial, men among them. Catarina Calandrino, a 40-year-old member of the Franciscan lay order, was denounced by 18 witnesses in 1624; her company had 26 or 27 members, and she was sentenced to be shut up for life in Palermo’s great hospital. Before a bishop’s court in 1619, Gracia la Chiaczisa of Sciacca described the ladies in one unforgettable line: “They look like people in front and empty on the back like the tiles of the roofs.”

    Henningsen reads all this as a Sicilian fairy cult with a “white” sabbath, a shared set of cultural dreams. He argues that the inquisitors turned the fairy into a witch: before the Inquisition, Sicily had no idea of the devil-worshipping witch. Was it shamanism? Henningsen says no, because no trance technique is described; others still compare it to shamanic cults. Either way the records show a cult of the 1500s and 1600s, not an unbroken line from antiquity.

    The evil eye. Sicilians call it or ; in the mountain town of Gratteri it’s l’ucchiatura. It isn’t only Sicilian: belief in it runs across southern Europe.

    Healing with prayers. Gratteri, in the Madonie mountains of the province of Palermo, kept its charms well into the last century. The historian Marco Fragale collected them from women born between 1869 and 1923. The , worm-charmers, were in his words “empirical doctors”. For a child with worms (pinworm, in medical terms) the healer drew crosses on the belly, spat three times and prayed, “San Pantaleu, San Pantaliuni, / Vui siti lu medicu di nostru Signuri”: Saint Pantaleon, you are the doctor of Our Lord. The charm then runs through Holy Week, day by day, to Easter Sunday. A necklace of seven garlic cloves helped, because l’agliu ammazza i viermi: garlic kills worms.

    For scantu, a fright, which was thought to throw the whole body off balance, the healer laid a hand on the chest, at “the mouth of the soul”, and seemed to fall into a trance while praying, three evenings running or once on a Friday, sometimes over a photograph of the patient. The words were secret, passed only to a trusted person of the opposite sex. Against the evil eye, women drew crosses on the forehead with the tongue, chanting “Quattru uocchi e quattru pisci, / ‘st’ucchiatura sinni sprisci” (four eyes and four fish, may this evil eye vanish), or dripped oil into a dish of water: if the stain spread, there was evil.

    The rites aren’t gone. Between 2002 and 2006 the researcher Napoli still met about 25 worm-charmers in five provinces. It is healing done with prayers.

    Against the evil eye, English collectors in the early 1900s also recorded coral, silver-bell rattles, the charm and the raised thumb and little finger, as a 2025 Palermo University Press study reports.

    Act 7

    The relic cabinet opens

    Time to open the cabinet. A relic is a saint’s body, a piece of it, or something that touched it, kept and honoured in a church. For most of Christian history a saint’s bones were no museum piece: they kept the saint present, and on the side of the town that held them. So towns wanted them, traded for them, and now and then stole them.

    Meet Lucy. Sicily’s other great virgin martyr is Lucy of Syracuse. By tradition she was killed in her home city in 304, under the emperor Diocletian, and her feast is 13 December. She is the patron of Syracuse and of sight, and medieval painters showed her carrying her eyes on a dish. Her life story is legend; even the Catholic Encyclopedia admitted in 1910 that it “cannot unfortunately be accepted without criticism”.

    One saint, two bodies. Here the cabinet gets crowded, because Lucy’s whole body is claimed by two cities. Venice says it came from Constantinople after the crusaders sacked that city in 1204; it lies today in the church of San Geremia, its face under a silver mask. Metz, in France, says a duke of Spoleto carried it off from Sicily and that it reached the abbey of St Vincent in 972. Syracuse, where she was buried, has the empty tomb, and borrows the Venetian body about once every ten years. Her head is claimed twice too. Thieves who stole the body in Venice in 1981 left the head behind; Bourges Cathedral, in France, says the Venetians gave it Lucy’s head in 1513. Both doubles are our own count, from sources that never compare notes.

    Agatha adds up. One tourism list counts 31 places outside Catania with a piece of her, yet where the parts can be counted, nothing is doubled: two thighbones in Catania, one breast in Catania and one in Galatina. Palermo Cathedral holds her arm.

    A king, boiled. Royalty was divided too. When King Louis IX of France died on crusade at Tunis in 1270, his body was dissected and boiled. His bones went to Saint-Denis, near Paris, and his entrails were buried at Monreale, near Palermo. Whether his heart is at Monreale as well is still argued.

    Palermo Cathedral says its Chapel of the Relics holds 17 reliquaries. No one has counted them for the whole island.

    Why Europe wanted bones. It wasn’t always so. Roman law banned selling martyrs’ bodies in 386. In 594 Pope Gregory the Great turned down an empress who wanted the head of St Paul: it is “not the custom of the Romans”, he wrote, “to presume to touch any part of the body”. He sent cloths that had lain near the saint’s tomb instead, with filings from St Peter’s chains, and said he could “scarcely believe” the Greeks dug up saints’ bones. Historians still argue how strict that Roman custom really was.

    Demand won. In 787 a Church council ruled that churches must have relics, and that a bishop who consecrated one without them should be deposed. Bones became precious, and in the Middle Ages they were bought, swapped and stolen. The historian Patrick Geary wrote a whole book, Furta Sacra (1978), on relic thefts and why medieval Christians so often approved of them. Catania’s homecoming of 1126 was one: its archbishop still calls it a “sacro furto”, a holy theft.

    So cutting up saints was common long before anyone wrote rules about it. When Rosalia’s bones turned up in 1624, Palermo sent pieces to other cities, to royal courts and to Pope Urban VIII, who reportedly wore one of her teeth on his chest. The Church mostly regulated the trade rather than stopping it. In 1215 a council forbade showing old relics outside their cases or selling them, and new relics needed the pope’s approval. In 1563 the Council of Trent told bishops to abolish “all filthy lucre”.

    The critics. Protestants thought the whole business a racket. In 1543 the reformer John Calvin published a Treatise on Relics; its full French title argues that Christendom would profit greatly from an inventory of every saint’s body and relic. Gather all the pieces of the True Cross, the cross Jesus died on, he joked, and you’d fill a good big boat. Every apostle had more than four bodies, each saint at least two or three, and he counted 14 nails from the Cross. You’ll often see him credited with a dozen heads of John the Baptist too. That count isn’t Calvin’s: it comes from a footnote by his 19th-century English translator, Valerian Krasinski.

    The rules today. Canon law now says: “It is absolutely forbidden to sell sacred relics.” The Vatican’s 2017 instruction bans trading them too, and says a saint’s body may not be cut up unless the bishop has Rome’s consent. It sorts relics into just two kinds: “significant” ones (the body, large parts of it, or all the ashes) and “non-significant” ones (small fragments, or objects that touched the saint).

    You may have met a three-tier ranking instead, from first-class relics (the body itself) down to third-class ones (cloths touched to a relic). It’s a popular devotional scheme, but the Church’s own rules don’t use it.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: first-, second- and third-class relics are Church lawWhat the record shows: the Vatican’s 2017 rules use only “significant” and “non-significant”

    Act 8

    To the Americas

    Sicily and Latin America both love candles and baroque gold. Is there a real connection? Some, through one empire: from 1516 to 1713 Sicily belonged to the Spanish crown.

    Benedict the Moor. Born at San Fratello to African parents who had been enslaved, he died at a convent in Palermo on 4 April 1589. He was beatified in 1743 and made a saint in 1807.

    His cult traveled with Black Catholic brotherhoods: a confraternity in Lisbon by 1609, and across Brazil and the Spanish and Portuguese New World from the early 1600s. In Venezuela his feast is danced to the chimbangueles drums.

    Antonio of Noto, another Sicilian holy man honored by the same brotherhoods, died at Noto in 1549 or 1550. In Brazil he is still venerated as Santo Antônio de Categeró.

    Rosalia crossed to New Spain with the Jesuits and the Spanish crown’s networks. And in 1555 the first Mexican Church council made Saint Joseph patron of “this new Church”.

    You’ll often read that Sicilian emigrants carried these saints to Argentina, Brazil and Venezuela. They got there centuries earlier, through Spain and Portugal.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Sicilian emigrants carried these saints to the AmericasWhat the record shows: they went earlier, through Spain and Portugal

    The shared look, the candles and the gold? No scholar we found traces it to one source. Votive candles are a habit of Catholics everywhere, and the baroque turned up the volume in both places. Nor did we find any sign that Mexico’s Day of the Dead came from Sicily, or Sicily’s from Mexico, or that St Joseph’s tables took root in Latin America.

    Curtain call

    So, no goddesses under the robes, and no ancient Egyptian cards. What Sicily has is better and stranger: a city that carried a veil against lava, a hermit elected patron before her bones were checked, a letter from Mary written 1,500 years late, tables for the poor, executed men prayed to as protectors, and healers the Inquisition couldn’t quite bring itself to burn. Not leftovers of someone else’s religion. Sicilians’ own.

    About these numbers

    Every number on this page comes from a table of checked figures. The research ran as many independent passes (different searches, different sources) whose results were cross-checked against each other: each figure needed two independent sources, preferably the original institution, book or journal. Where sources disagree, the page shows a range or names the disagreement: 1071–72 for Palermo’s fall, “about 1040” for Agatha’s removal, about 6,000 to 7,000 people tried, 25 to 52 executions.

    “Dozens tried” for the donne di fuora is deliberate: counts run from 65 to 77 to 193, depending on what is counted (people in the surviving reports, one historian’s charges of contact with the dead, perhaps every woman named). Counts that come from a single document name that document in the sentence: Pitrè’s survey, the Sicilian Region’s 2013 register, Pitrè’s tally of painted tablets, Napoli’s worm-charmers, the collectors in Intorre’s study, Palermo Cathedral’s 17 reliquaries. The relic drawers are what the sources report, not an inventory; “two claims” for Lucy’s body and head is our own comparison. No survey of evil-eye belief in Sicily turned up, so the page says nothing about how many Sicilians hold it today. Beliefs are written as beliefs.

    The myth-check stamps mark claims that circulate widely and that the record does not support. A stamp means “no evidence found”, never “proven false”, unless it says so.

    Pictures

    • Saint Rosalia: Anthony van Dyck, Saint Rosalie Interceding for the Plague-stricken of Palermo, 1624 (detail). The Met, 71.41. CC0.
    • Rosalia’s car: Jean Houël, The car of Saint Rosalia, aquatint, 1780s. Wellcome Collection, 7145i. Public Domain Mark.
    • Saint Agatha: Saint Agatha, bronze statuette, Italian (probably Naples), mid-17th c. The Met, 197071. CC0.
    • A reliquary bust: Reliquary Bust of Saint Juliana, circle of Giovanni di Bartolo, c. 1376. The Met, 61.266. CC0. A stand-in: Agatha’s own bust in Catania is by Giovanni di Bartolo.
    • Saint Lucy: Francisco de Zurbarán, Saint Lucy, c. 1625/30. National Gallery of Art, 1943.7.11. Public domain.
    • Saint Joseph: St. Joseph, crèche figure, attributed to Salvatore di Franco, Naples, 2nd half 18th c. The Met, 64.164.3a–c. CC0.
    • A goddess: Terracotta bust (Persephone or Demeter), Greek, made in Sicily, 4th c. BCE. The Met, 1994.600.1–.2. CC0.
    • Isis: Statuette of Isis nursing Horus, Egyptian, Late Period, 664–332 BCE. The Met, 553002. CC0.
    • A Palermo jar: Albarello (pharmacy jar), Lazzaro workshop, Palermo, 2nd half 16th c. The Met, 188537. CC0. Its foliage also makes the tile wall.
    • The proscenium: Gilt ripple frame, Sicilian(?), late 17th c. The Met, 1975.1.2326. CC0.

    • An angel: Angel, crèche figure, Naples, 2nd half 18th c. The Met (crèche angels, 64.164). CC0.
